A bare typed price carries no vintage at all -- it just sits there looking current. (b) was the middle road and was not taken: it needs a threshold nobody can defend (why 6 hours and not 18?) and it would have added a second, time-based invalidation axis beside the stamp, which is more machinery than the problem is worth. || THE STAMP IS KEPT EVEN THOUGH THE PRICE MAPS ARE DROPPED, and a test pins it: without `scanId` a restored pick lands in a null-stamped slice and reads as EMPTY, silently undoing the one thing this persists for. || IN-SESSION BEHAVIOUR IS UNCHANGED and that is deliberate -- all four caches still live in the store while the tab is open, so a step-6 -> step-7 round trip still keeps a typed limit (spec test 11's first half). What is dropped is survival across a RELOAD. || THREE TESTS, MUTATION-VERIFIED HERE rather than asserted: one checks the BLOB itself and not merely what reads back (a price never written cannot be restored by a later change to `merge`), one pins that the pick still comes back, one pins the stamp. Reverting `partialize` to persist the whole slice fails 1; dropping the stamp from `persistableCardEdits` fails 3. || BUILT BUT NOT YET ADVERSARIALLY AUDITED -- it is a persisted-shape change and gets its own round, together with build step 3.

decisions.q: Phase G build step 2 was written by a PARALLEL SESSION and appeared in this container's working tree after commit d1ccecbd, with mtimes preserved from another machine. It was preserved at 53b43844 and then audited at its own scope. Round 1 returned ZERO gate-level findings. What was fixed, and what is Kenneth's to decide?
decisions.a: THREE FIXED, ALL THE SAME GENRE STEP 1'S AUDIT FOUND. || (1) A FALSE COMMENT ON THE ONE PATH THAT COULD PUT A WRONG NUMBER ON A BROKER ORDER. writeCardEdit drops a write when there is no scan to stamp it with, and its comment said 'Dropping it is at least visible: the field reverts in front of the user.' THE AUDIT PROVED THAT FALSE BY EXPERIMENT -- strip the stamp from the step-7 fixture and the card still reads $2.71 while the arm request carries limit_price 2.5. TradeCard owns its overlay and re-syncs only on a symbol, contract or resetKey change, so a dropped write reverts nothing. The PATH IS STILL UNREACHABLE -- currentScanIdFor is null only for a result carrying neither scan_id nor timestamp, both are backend-unconditional, and step 7's cards come only from scanResult.candidates -- so the code is unchanged and the COMMENT now says the safety is unreachability rather than visibility, and names what would break it. A comment that tells the next person a live hazard is self-correcting is worse than no comment. || (2) THE GUARD DEVIATION 3 RESTS ON WAS PINNED BY NOTHING. The [scanResult] effect no longer clears the edit caches -- the stamp does -- but it still bumps scanEpoch, which reaches TradeCard as resetKey and rebuilds the overlay. Deleting that bump left all 24 step-7 tests green. It sits directly on the display-vs-send axis: without it the slice empties on a new scan while the card keeps rendering the old value. ONE TEST ADDED that asserts BOTH HALVES in one run -- the number on screen and the number on the wire, after the same scan lands -- and MUTATION-TESTED HERE: removing the bump fails it and fails nothing else. || (3) normalizeCardEdits claimed the worst a bad entry could do was 'render as an untouched field'. False: the readers fall back with `??`, which catches only null and undefined, so a string would reach limit_price and PortfolioPosition.stop AS A STRING. The three PRICE maps are now value-checked to a finite number or null -- null IS 'untouched', so the claim is made TRUE rather than retracted. Two tests, mutation-verified. Only reachable from an externally corrupted localStorage blob, so this is cheap insurance, and the remaining shape-only gap on picks/maxLossOverride is now stated in the code instead of implied away. || THE THREE DECLARED DEVIATIONS ALL HOLD, checked rather than accepted. STAMP-DERIVED: TradeCardData carries no scan_id, so every call site would have read it back out of the store -- the parameter bought nothing. TIMESTAMP-FALLBACK: scan_id really did enter ScanResult at ac84e93d on 2026-08-28 with no backfill, and both producers are datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat() -- MICROSECOND precision, so two scans cannot share a timestamp and it is a working stamp rather than a sentinel. NO-EFFECT-RESET: the effect does run on mount, StoreHydration restores result and slices together, and a reset there would destroy a restored pick -- with the gap that its replacement guard was untested, which is fix (2) above. || ONE ITEM IS KENNETH'S, NOT A DEFECT: see phase_g_step2_followups G2-5. Persisting the edit caches removes the page unmount that used to clear them, so a typed entry limit now survives indefinitely under one scan_id. The stamp catches a NEW SCAN, not the passage of TIME. Three options are written down with the question. || ALSO CORRECTED: this file's step 2 note said '117 suites / 1473 passed' and 'the 54 new ones (34 + 20)'. Measured here: 1474 and 55 (34 + 21). The commit message had it right and the single source of truth did not.

decisions.q: Spec S5's draft signature is `setCardPick(mode, scanId, key, pick)` -- the caller passes the stamp. Keep it?
decisions.a: NO. The shipped signature is `setCardEdit(mode, field, key, value)`, and `currentScanIdFor(state, mode)` is the SINGLE derivation shared by the writer and the reader, so the two cannot disagree. A caller that passes a stale scanId writes an edit under a stamp the reader rejects -- an edit that silently vanishes, which is the very class of defect the stamp exists to make impossible. And no caller has a better source than the store: TradeCardData carries no scan_id, so every call site would have read scanResult?.scan_id back out of the store anyway. The parameter bought nothing and cost a way to get it wrong. || ONE GENERIC WRITER covers all five maps, so the spec's setCardPick(mode, key, pick) is setCardEdit(mode, 'picks', key, pick). Five near-identical setters is how a sixth gets added that forgets to stamp.
decisions.provenance: Taken while building step 2, before any call site existed. The spec's signature was followed far enough to see what a caller would have to pass, and the answer was 'the thing the store already knows'.

decisions.q: The stamp is scan_id (spec S5). What should a write do when the result in the store has no scan_id?
decisions.a: FALL BACK TO `timestamp`, DO NOT DROP THE EDIT. This is reachable, not hypothetical: scan_id entered the frontend's ScanResult on 2026-08-28 (ac84e93d) and NO store migration backfills it, so a localStorage blob written before that date restores a result without one. With no stamp every card edit is dropped WHILE THE CARD STILL DISPLAYS IT -- the user types $2.71, the card shows $2.71, and the order carries the card's original $2.50. That display-vs-send disagreement is the exact defect class step 7 has spent four rounds closing, and it is strictly worse than the staleness the stamp prevents. || timestamp is required on both result types, predates scan_id, and CHANGES PER SCAN, so it is a working stamp and not a sentinel that matches everything -- there is a test for that. Null is left only for a result carrying neither, which is not a result. An EMPTY-STRING id is also treated as no stamp, for the same 'never matches everything' reason test 15 names.
decisions.provenance: Surfaced by two step-7 test fixtures that built scanResult as `{candidates: [...]} as any`. The fixtures were lying about a required field and were fixed -- but the question they raised (what does a real result with no id do?) had a real answer, and `git log -S` on the type is what turned it from speculation into a date.

decisions.q: Spec S5.1 ends: 'Keep the page's [scanResult] effect exactly as it is ... add [maxLossOverrideBySymbol] while you are there.' Once the four edit caches move into the store there are no setState hooks left for that effect to call. Add a store-level reset action in their place, or remove the clears?
decisions.a: REMOVE THEM, AND EXPORT NO RESET ACTION AT ALL. S5.1's last clause is WRONG, and following it would have introduced the bug the design exists to prevent. That effect ALSO RUNS ON MOUNT, where scanResult has not changed at all -- and on mount the slice may legitimately hold edits StoreHydration has just restored alongside the very result they were stamped against. A blanket reset there destroys a restored pick on EVERY PAGE LOAD. It would have passed test 11's 'does not survive a new scan' half while failing test 11b's second half, which is the half that exists to stop exactly this. || The three FETCHED caches (estimatesByContract, structuralBySymbol, exitPlanByContract) still clear there: they are still local useState and nothing stamps them. The four EDIT caches do not, because the stamp already invalidates by every path that lands a result rather than only the ones someone remembered to wire -- which is S5.1's own argument turned on S5.1's own last sentence. || maxLossOverrideBySymbol's omission IS fixed, structurally rather than by adding a line: it now shares ONE slice and ONE stamp with the other three, so there is no list left for it to be dropped off. That is a better answer to 'an omission, not a decision' than remembering to add it -- the next person cannot forget, because there is nothing to remember. || If you are about to add a reset action: re-read S5.1's two failed drafts, and note that clearPickedContracts, this store's existing fossil of that approach, still has zero production callers.
decisions.provenance: Found while building step 2, by asking what the effect does on mount rather than on a new scan. Not raised by any audit.

decisions.q: Phase G build step 1 (6c15d338) was audited adversarially at the audit_rule v2 gate. Round 1 returned ZERO gate-level findings, which per the rule ENDS THE LOOP at one round. Twelve below-gate findings came with it. Which of those get fixed in-branch, given that the rule says below-gate findings are logged against main and NOT fixed here?
decisions.a: THREE, AND ONLY BECAUSE OF WHAT THEY WERE, NOT BECAUSE THEY WERE CHEAP. The rule's purpose is to stop a branch widening under audit pressure, and each of these three sits inside the module step 1 exists to deliver. || (1) THE GUARD DID NOT KEEP ITS OWN PROMISE. routers/portfolio.py wraps the rr_ratios config read in a try/except, and the comment beside it says why in so many words: every send path places the broker order FIRST and persists second, so an exception there does not prevent a trade, it LOSES THE RECORD of a trade that already happened -- a real filled position with no stop and no TP alert. But the guard covered the LOAD only. A malformed-but-loadable value (`rr_ratios: 2.0`, a scalar where a list belongs) loads clean and then raises TypeError out of the slice in _seed_for_rr, producing that exact 500. Reproduced before fixing. Two ways out: fix the code, or fix the comment. Fixing the comment would have left a known hole behind a sentence saying it was closed, so seed_tp_from_pick is now TOTAL in rr_ratios and the comment is true. || (2) AND (3) TWO MUTATION GAPS IN STEP 1'S OWN TESTS. The audit deleted the `<= 0` half of the gating precondition and all 33 tests stayed green; same for the bool guard in _rr_ratio_for_row. Tests are step 1's deliverable, so a hole in them is unfinished work, not new scope. Three tests added, and EACH WAS MUTATION-TESTED BY ME rather than taken from the audit: M2 now fails 3, M9 fails 1, the new isinstance guard fails 4. || THE OTHER NINE ARE LOGGED, NOT FIXED -- phase_g_step1_followups. The two genuinely tempting ones were left alone on purpose: the PATCH path can still write half the pair (pre-existing, and the create-path claim it narrows was earned on the create path), and `gt=0` accepts Infinity (a whole-schema hole entryPrice has had since long before G). Both are main's, and fixing either here would be exactly the widening the rule forbids. || A SEPARATE THING HAPPENED THAT IS NOT A FIX: A FALSE CLAIM WAS RETRACTED. Step 1's code comment, its commit message, spec S4.2 and this file all asserted that omitting one of the five `aliases` entries would SILENTLY drop the pick. It would not. populate_by_name plus Field(alias=...) on every field means pydantic takes both conventions unaided, and FastAPI validates with model_validate, which bypasses that __init__ entirely -- verified by construction both ways, with the entries removed. The entries are KEPT for symmetry with the eleven above them; all three documents now say they are not load-bearing. The commit message cannot be edited and is wrong where it stands; this record is the correction. Same genre, same day: the '4 tests' figure for the option-price mutation is really 2. || WHAT THE AUDIT CONFIRMED SOUND, so no one re-treads it: all eight rows of S4.3's table one at a time; that exitPlan.targets[].price is UNDERLYING space for OPTION positions too (contracts.py:1079-1082 builds it from entry_price, the underlying; the premium lives in the sibling contractPrice field) -- which was the single highest-value question, since it is the one input path the module cannot refuse by signature; that add_position is the ONLY PortfolioPositionModel construction site in the backend; `alembic heads` really returns one head; and that the migration's five column names match the model byte-for-byte.

decisions.q: Found while building G's step 1, not by review: spec section 4.3 claims a THREE-WAY AGREEMENT (alert, label, drawer) as the acceptance criterion for its tests. Does the drawer actually hold up its end?
decisions.a: NO, NOT UNDER A NON-DEFAULT rr_ratios. EditDrawer.tsx:1310-1325's tpMethodOptions looks its rows up with HARDCODED LITERALS -- `exitPlan?.targets.find(t => t.rrRatio === rr)` called as rowPrice(2) and rowPrice(3), with labels '2R plan' / '3R plan' to match. With rr_ratios [1.5, 4.0], the backend mapping that spec test 3 REQUIRES seeds exit_plan_2r from the 1.5R row and TP_HIT fires there correctly, while the drawer finds no row at rrRatio === 2, renders '2R plan' as the selected method with a NULL PRICE beside it, and mislabels a 1.5R row as 2R when it does resolve. || TWO SITES, NOT ONE -- the second found by step 1's audit, 2026-09-14, and verified by hand. The paragraph above is the READ side. The WRITE side is EditDrawer.tsx:602-603, in the exit-plan recompute's restamp: `const rr = active === 'exit_plan_2r' ? 2 : active === 'exit_plan_3r' ? 3 : null`, then `plan.targets.find(t => t.rrRatio === rr)`. Under rr_ratios [1.5, 4.0] with exit_plan_2r active, that find matches nothing, rowPrice is null, and tpMethodPatch is NOT included in the patch -- while exitPlan in the SAME patch IS replaced. resolved_tp_price then keeps pointing at a row of the PREVIOUS plan and TP_HIT fires on a price no longer in the plan on screen. That is worse than the read side's null label: a stale number that still fires. STEP 3 MUST CHANGE BOTH -- fixing only :1310-1325 leaves this one hardcoded. Still not blocking, for the same measured reason: risk_rules.yaml ships [2.0, 3.0] and no frontend caller passes the stocks rr_ratios override.
decisions.why_it_is_G_s_to_own: Before G, active_tp_method was written by the drawer ALONE, and the drawer only ever offered rows it could find at rrRatio 2 and 3 -- so the inconsistent state was UNREACHABLE. G adds the first writer that can produce it. This is not a pre-existing bug G merely sits next to.
decisions.why_it_is_not_blocking: MEASURED, not assumed. Nothing reaches it today: the options exit plan is built only from config (routers/contracts.py:1024), risk_rules.yaml ships rr_ratios [2.0, 3.0], and although /api/stocks/exit-plan accepts a per-request rr_ratios override (stock_scan.py:1578, 1-5 entries) NO FRONTEND CALLER PASSES ONE -- api.ts:523 declares the field and nothing sets it. It becomes reachable the moment either changes.
decisions.the_fix_and_where: BUILD STEP 3 (the card, section 6), because it is frontend work on the surface that step already touches: the drawer must read the configured ratios POSITIONALLY the way the backend mapping now does, and label rows from those ratios rather than from the enum names. DO NOT 'fix' the backend to match the drawer by hardcoding 2.0/3.0 -- spec test 3 exists precisely to fail that, and the enum names are row ORDINALS whose names predate the ratios being configurable.

decisions.q: Spec section 11 item 5, the one item that BLOCKED half of G's build: Q5 says an explicit method pick is required before a trade can be sent, and S5 -- the after-scan auto-executor at step-4-stocks/page.tsx:196 -- sends with, in its own words, 'no human in the loop'. Those cannot both hold as written. The collision is STRUCTURAL, not incidental: spec section 5 clears picks when a new scan lands, and S5 fires ON a new scan, against candidates that did not exist when any pick was made. A PICK CAN NEVER EXIST FOR AN S5 TRADE. Three options, costed in spec section 7.3: (a) S5 is exempt and says so; (b) S5 is gated, which disables it; (c) S5 arms a method alongside the symbol.
decisions.a: (a) S5 IS EXEMPT, AND SAYS SO. Auto-execute keeps working exactly as it does today. The positions it creates pass no picked_* fields, so picked_method is NULL -- which the portfolio already renders as an em-dash and which section 4.3's last table row already seeds as ('ladder', NULL). NO NEW CODE IS REQUIRED to make this work; what is required is that the section 7.2 gate is NOT extended to that call site, and that a test pins BOTH halves (test 9b: a position IS created, and it does NOT raise the gate).
decisions.what_it_costs: Q5's guarantee is no longer universal, and the spec now says so IN THE DECISION ITSELF rather than only in section 7.3: section 3.5 was rewritten from 'nothing goes out on a default nobody looked at' to 'nothing A HUMAN SENDS goes out on a default nobody looked at'. That rewording is the whole cost of (a), and leaving it unwritten was the trap -- a reader who takes the original sentence literally concludes S5 is gated, and it is not.
decisions.why_not_b_or_c: (b) holds Q5 literally but DISABLES A WORKING FEATURE as a side effect: S5's precondition can never be met, so after-scan auto-execute would stop creating positions entirely. That is a real product change hiding inside a consistency argument. (c) keeps the feature and satisfies Q5's letter by arming a method alongside the symbol, but it is a pick made against numbers that DO NOT EXIST YET -- precisely what section 6.1's staleness reset exists to prevent. It would manufacture the appearance of a decision rather than a decision.
decisions.regression_risk: The danger is now in the OPPOSITE direction: a later implementer extending the section 7.2 gate to S5 'for consistency' silently re-creates option (b) and disables auto-execute, and nothing else in the suite would catch it. Test 9b's 'a position IS created' half is that regression test. Do not delete it as redundant.

The Sell-to-Close per-row 'edited' badge is unrelated and stays. NOT YET BUILT.

decisions.q: firstPassage.targets in the Final Recommendation's monte_carlo branch is ungated vintage. Gate it or not?

The branch may then render nothing until Estimate is clicked, which is accepted -- consistency with how the rest of the card treats stale numbers wins. decisions.q: SPEC DEVIATION raised by round 3: the schematic's card 03 puts the dollars-left ON the badge and per SHARE ('Caution - 71% of premium - $1.49 left'); what shipped kept the badge percent-only with per-CONTRACT dollars on the headline below. Which?
decisions.a: MATCH THE SCHEMATIC. The badge now reads '<pct>% of premium - $<x.xx>/share left'. Reason it matters beyond this card: the badge is what the ranking view will reuse, and there it would travel with only a percentage -- the half that does not say whether being wrong costs $8 or $800. Two consequences accepted deliberately: (1) the card now shows the same quantity twice in two units a foot apart (per share on the badge, per contract on the headline), so both strings name their unit; (2) '/share' rather than the schematic's bare '$1.49 left' because StatusBadge uppercases its label and is white-space:nowrap -- the CONTENT follows the schematic, the CASING follows the design system. AMENDED IN ROUND 6: the badge also leads with the VERDICT WORD ('CAUTION - 71% of premium - $1.49/share left'), which the schematic always had and round 5's first build dropped -- StatusBadge renders `label ?? STATUS_LABEL[status]`, so supplying a label REPLACES the word. Without it, two cards printing the same rounded percentage on opposite sides of the pass line differed only by colour. BUILT.

decisions.q: Round 6 verified that the card's edited Invalidation, Max fill and Time stop never reach a send path. Fix inside this branch, or record it and build later?
decisions.a: FIX NOW, INSIDE THIS BRANCH. Threaded the two fields that have consumers: Invalidation (becomes PortfolioPosition.stop, drives STOP_REACHED against the live underlying price) and Entry limit (posted as the broker order's limit_price on the quick Place Limit path and in AutoTradeArm, and shown in the button label). TradeCard's premiumStopTouchedRef generalised to a per-field TouchedFields map, so an untouched field caches null and keeps deferring to the live card value as mergePlan moves it -- the same rule piece 4 established for the premium stop. Max fill and Time stop NOT threaded: they have no consumer to thread them to, so it is a build, not a fix (see open questions).

decisions.q: The schematic (card 03) puts the dollars-left ON the badge and per SHARE ('Caution . 71% of premium . $1.49 left'). Shipped keeps the badge percent-only with per-CONTRACT dollars on the line beneath. Change it or keep it?
decisions.a: SUPERSEDED BY ITS OWN PREMISE BEING FALSE -- corrected in round 7, NOT by Kenneth; he needs to confirm or overrule this correction. The answer recorded here claimed 'Verified both are on screen: the badge prints the verdict word plus "N% OF PREMIUM"'. That verification was never true. formatStopLossBadge (lib/risk.ts) returns 'CAUTION - 71% of premium - $1.49/share left' -- the per-share dollars-left IS on the badge, so the premise ('shipped keeps the badge percent-only') described a code state that does not exist, and the follow-on note ('the per-share left is not printed') is false too. The question it re-asked had already been answered the other way by BADGE-SPEC-2026-09-05 ('MATCH THE SCHEMATIC ... BUILT'), which is what actually shipped and what round 6 then amended to lead with the verdict word. Two mutually exclusive decisions on one question, same date, and the later one edited the authoritative schematic to match a code state that never shipped. ACTION TAKEN IN ROUND 7: the schematic's card 03 has been put back to the badge the code produces and carries a CORRECTED note saying why; BADGE-SPEC-2026-09-05 stands as the live decision. No code changed -- the code was right throughout.

decisions.q: Card 03 heads the section 'Stop cost' and says every other line stays as it reads today; shipped reads 'MAX LOSS IF THE STOP IS HIT' (approved as NOTATION-2026-09-04 but never recorded as a departure). Amend the schematic, or revert the header?
decisions.a: AMEND THE SCHEMATIC. The shipped header stands.

decisions.q: Should a PREMIUM_STOP alert stamp the threshold it fired at, rather than the Alerts page resolving it live from the position (so editing a position silently relabels its historical alert rows with a threshold those alerts never used)?
decisions.a: YES -- the alert should show the threshold it actually fired at. APPROVED, NOT STARTED. Cross-cutting: a field on the toast, a persisted alertStore migration, and the same field from the backend generator's websocket path. Raised by round 5; the lossy Math.round on that label was already fixed there.

decisions.q: Thread the card's Max fill and Time stop through to a send path as well?
decisions.a: DEFERRED, confirmed by Kenneth. Neither has a consumer today, so it is a build (new persisted field, backend column, alert change), not the wiring fix Invalidation and Entry limit were. Stays an open question rather than being half-done inside an audit branch.

decisions.q: Round 7 finding 3: Max fill and Time stop render with the SAME click-to-edit affordance as the three fields that now reach the broker, but nothing anywhere consumes either one. Thread them, signal them, or leave them?
decisions.a: MADE READ-ONLY in round 7, pending Kenneth. Threading stays deferred (MAXFILL-TIMESTOP-2026-09-05 -- it is a build: a persisted field, a backend column and an alert change). But shipping two inert fields that look identical to three load-bearing ones was not part of that deferral, it was an omission: before this branch all five were inert and at least consistent. Both rows are now plain KV rows (the schematic draws them as plain fields, so this is not a spec deviation). REVERSIBLE in one line each if Kenneth would rather keep the affordance and add a marker instead.

decisions.q: Round 7 finding 4: the Invalidation field became PortfolioPosition.stop (compared against the live underlying by STOP_REACHED) while keeping min=0.01, no max and no directional check. Bound it?
decisions.a: BOUNDED, directionally, in round 7. Bullish: [50%, 99%] of the card's stock price. Bearish: [101%, 150%]. Clamps rather than rejects, matching the Premium stop field Round 5 bounded for the same reason. Deliberately WIDE -- it is there to reject a mistyped digit, not a wide stop. The two failures it closes on a $145 stock: '1400' fires a Critical STOP_REACHED (plus Gmail and Telegram) on the first 30s scan; '14' is worse because it is silent -- the send gate only requires a positive number, so the trade goes out believing it is protected by a level the underlying will never reach.

decisions.q: Round 7 finding 6: touchedRef was a one-way latch -- once a field was typed it was pinned for the life of Step 7 and mergePlan could no longer reach it. Round 6's own note calls 'a card with no way back to inheriting' the bad outcome. Add a way back?
decisions.a: YES -- clearing the input reverts the field to the plan's value and clears its touched flag, the same gesture the portfolio EditDrawer already uses to mean 'inherit the global'. Chosen over a revert button or a line of copy so it adds no control to a schematic-governed card and does not pre-empt EDITED-FLAG-2026-09-04, which is Kenneth's and still unbuilt. Surfaced only as an input tooltip, so it is undiscoverable until you hover -- the edited indicator is the right place to fix that properly.

decisions.q: Round 8 finding 2: an out-of-range entry in the card's three bounded fields was CLAMPED. On a $150 bullish card '1400' typed for '140' clamped to $148.50 -- 1% below spot -- stored as PortfolioPosition.stop, so STOP_REACHED fires Critical on the first intraday wiggle while the user believes the stop is 7% away. Clamp or reject?
decisions.a: REJECT, in round 8. Out of range now leaves the field's previous value on screen and reports nothing, which is the position the portfolio EditDrawer's premium-stop editor already took on the identical question ('showing the previous value back is the honest answer'). Two editors in one branch with opposite policies, and the card had the unsafe one on the field that becomes the position's stop. A clamp does not refuse a fat-finger, it renames it. Side benefit: this retires round 6's seed-outside-bounds hazard at the source -- the clamp was what made a bare focus-and-blur look like a deliberate edit when the SEED itself sat outside the bounds. REVERSES the clamp behaviour round 5 chose for the Premium stop field.

decisions.q: Round 8's CRITICAL: the Entry limit became the order's limit_price in this branch and was the only threaded field left unbounded (min=0.01, no max). Nothing else gates it -- checkTradeRisk and the capital-at-risk row both size off contractDetails.mid, and the backend's limit_price is an unvalidated Optional[float].
decisions.a: BOUNDED to [0.25x, 3x] of the live-or-scan mid. Of the three threaded fields this is the only one whose fat-finger is an EXECUTION error rather than an alerting one: on a $2.50 mid, '25.0' typed for '2.50' posted limit_price 25.0 on a BUY/OPEN order, and on a wide options book a marketable buy limit an order of magnitude above the ask is a real fill at a real price. Deliberately wider than the other two fields because paying up through the ask is a legitimate use of a limit order -- 3x catches the missing decimal point (10x) with room to spare.

decisions.q: Round 8 finding 3: the field bounds were anchored to data.price / contractDetails.mid, which come off scanResult -- and scanStore persists that to localStorage, so after a reload they can be days old.
decisions.a: ANCHORED ON THE LIVE QUOTE, falling back to the scan-time figures. The page already fetches both and renders them as 'Live stock:' and 'Live mid:' a few rows from the fields; they were simply never handed down. Without this, AAPL scanned at $145 and reopened at $200 rejected every sane stop below today's spot.

decisions.q: Standing since the round 6 handoff, asked three times: the loop has caught regressions from its own prior rounds four times and ten rounds have produced no clean result. Does that change how many clean rounds this branch needs, or does the exit criterion itself need to change?
decisions.a: THE CRITERION CHANGES. Two measurements settled it. (1) Findings per round are FLAT -- 11, 13, 14, ~4, 11, 11, 17, 13, 17, 14 -- while lines added per fix round are also flat at ~500 (474, 648, 713, 125, 480, 230, 642, 550, 1156, 496). Each round audits a diff whose newest commit has never been reviewed; rounds 8 and 9 say so in their own commit messages. A round cannot come back clean while the previous round's fix sits inside the audit target. That is arithmetic, not bad luck. (2) The count is flat but SEVERITY has collapsed. Rounds 1-9 produced three CRITICALs that all reached money (a card posting a stop it was not showing; limit_price 25.0 on a $2.50 contract; a typed stop re-anchored ABOVE spot, firing Critical STOP_REACHED with Gmail and Telegram behind it). Round 10's headline finding is a backend guard the frontend already blocks -- defense-in-depth, unreachable by any user of this app -- and of its fourteen findings exactly one (the missing v3->v4 bump) could damage real data. NEW PROCEDURE: freeze HEAD; run a REPORT-ONLY round that is forbidden to write code; triage the findings as a batch; fix only what clears the gate above; log the rest as issues against main. Merge when one round clears the gate. Also noted, not chosen: the scope grew mid-loop -- THREAD-EDITS-2026-09-05 added three editable fields, three page-level caches, a backend flag and a migration at round 6, so rounds 7-10 were the FIRST audit of a new feature, not a re-audit of Phase D.

decisions.q: First round under AUDIT-EXIT-CRITERION-2026-09-05: HEAD frozen, auditor forbidden to write code, findings triaged as a batch against the severity gate.
decisions.a: 1 GATE, 12 FOLLOW-UP -- the first round whose findings were mostly below the gate. GATE: the Portfolio drawer's 'Fires at premium $X' preview named a price the alert does NOT fire at, on ~3% of ordinary positions and in the dangerous direction (claiming the stop arms a cent EARLIER than it does). `Math.floor(t * 100) / 100` performs a second float op and `t * 100` lands exactly on its integer for some inputs: entry $4.00 at 7% gives t = 3.7199999999999998, printed '$3.72', arms at $3.71. Reachable by typing 7 in the drawer. VERIFIED independently before fixing. Fixed by a shared `premiumStopFiringPrice` in lib/premiumStop.ts. NOTE: writing a SWEEP test rather than another single-pair one immediately exposed the mirror trap -- `t * 100` also lands BELOW its integer (a $0.57 threshold whose product is 56.99999999999999 floors to $0.56), so a bare floor is wrong in both directions; the helper rounds to nearest then steps back only when that cent exceeds the threshold. The prior test (round 9's) had the right shape but pinned one lucky pair, which is the lesson worth keeping: a single hand-picked example cannot establish a float property.

decisions.decision: Round 13 CLEARS the severity gate: 0 GATE findings, 10 FOLLOW-UP. Phase D and both riding already_shipped items are now audit_clean=true after 13 rounds. The two boundary calls the auditor flagged as arguable (F2's $0.00 preview, F4's pre-edit invalidation read) were re-verified against the code this session before accepting the classing -- per the standing trap, an audit finding is not trusted without a file:line checked first-hand, and that applies to a finding classed DOWN as much as up. The severity gate introduced by AUDIT-EXIT-CRITERION-2026-09-05 worked: it converged in one round after twelve that could not.

The three round-12 FOLLOW-UPs with user-visible consequences are FIXED on a branch restarted off main, as one capped batch. (2) The basket path's dropped-stop disclosure and its hard-rejection banner rendered inside step-7's `{selectedBroker && ...}` block, which the basket never sets -- both are hoisted to the paper-execution section itself, and two page-level tests drive a basket submit with NO broker selected (both fail against the old JSX). `paperOrderId` stays inside the gate; only the two direct paths set it. (5) EditField's empty-draft message said 'Enter 0 to clear this level' on all four of its call sites (Stop, Structural stop, Contracts, Current price -- EditField is not exported and has no other), including the two where 0 clears nothing: Contracts (0 stores 1 while the box goes on showing 0) and Current price (0 writes currentPrice: 0 and pnlPct: -100). A `zeroClears` prop makes the invitation opt-in and REVERTS a 0 where it is off; a post-commit resync also puts `stored` back whenever the call site normalises a committed value (Contracts 0.4 -> 1), which closes the same display-vs-store split by its other route. The handoff called this one a likely misclassification and it reads that way -- a -100% P&L on the row is a wrong number in front of a user -- but the distinction is moot now that it is fixed. (13) The two editors of `premiumStopPct` disagreed on what counts as a stop: TradeCard refuses a dollar below 10% of the mid while the drawer accepted 0.01%. Both now derive from PREMIUM_STOP_MIN_PCT/PREMIUM_STOP_MAX_PCT in lib/premiumStop.ts (0.10/0.99), chosen to match the GLOBAL stop's own `ge=0.10, le=1.0`. Direction of unification follows the card's precedent, which is the argued one. The drawer's reverts also SAY WHY now -- every rejecting path in PremiumStopEditor was silent. NOT changed: the backend's `gt=0, lt=1` per-position bound. It is the outer bound, and legacy rows below the new floor still have to load and be editable upward (pinned by a test). This NARROWS round 13's F2 ('Fires at premium $0.00'): the typed route is gone, but audit round 1 found two the band does not govern -- a legacy stored row, and the GLOBAL, which Settings offers at 100% and risk_settings.py accepts (le=1.0). F2 stays open.

Adversarial round 1 on the batch commit (1e4afb84, frozen, report-only): 0 GATE, 16 FOLLOW-UP. Under AUDIT-EXIT-CRITERION-2026-09-05 that clears the gate, so the batch is DONE at one round of the two it was capped at. Eight findings were fixed anyway, in a second commit, on a narrower rule than the gate: a defect THIS batch introduced, cheap and contained, is finishing the fix rather than widening it. Those eight: (1) PremiumStopEditor.commit had no `if (!dirtyRef.current)` guard, so a row stored outside the new band showed the new rejection on a bare focus-and-blur -- accusing the user of a value they never typed; (2) the card converted the band to dollars with round-to-nearest, so its OWN boundary values fell outside the band ($5.24 mid -> min 9.92%, $1.01 mid -> max 99.01%) -- now `premiumStopDollarBounds` in premiumStop.ts, rounding inward, pinned by a cent-by-cent sweep from $0.02 to $50 plus the degenerate $0.01 mid; (4) handleSubmit cleared saveNotes but not orderError, so a successful basket rendered the previous submit's 'Some orders were not saved' -- unreachable before the hoist, reachable because of it; (9) the drawer's new rejection message never cleared on an external change (30s sync, another client), leaving a caution attached to a value no longer on screen -- fixed in BOTH editors; (14) the band was advertised only in the inheriting hint branch, i.e. not on the position being edited when the bound is hit; (6)(7)(12) three comments this batch introduced that assert something their code does not, plus the '(0,1) stays for legacy rows' premise finding 3 disproved; (11)(16) the 'five fields' miscount and the lost trailing newline in this file.

Adversarial round 2, on c8152847 (the round-1 FIX commit, frozen): 0 GATE, 15 FOLLOW-UP. Both rounds of the cap are now spent. Round 2's central result is that the criterion's own prediction landed on the first attempt: c8152847 introduced TWO user-visible regressions in the arithmetic it added. (a) `premiumStopDollarBounds` did `Math.ceil(mid * 0.10 * 100)` in binary floats, so on every dime-multiple mid -- exactly where 10% IS expressible at 2dp -- it climbed a whole cent: a $3.00 mid demanded $0.31 = 10.33% where the drawer accepts $0.30. 172 mids between $0.02 and $50. (b) Rounding the minimum UP put the card's SEED (round(mid x global, 2), round-to-nearest) below the card's own minimum, and `EditableKV.save` ran its range check ABOVE its no-op guard -- so a bare focus-and-blur printed 'Must be between $0.53 and $5.18' for a value nobody typed. At a global of 0.10 that went from 3 of 4999 cent-mids to 2184. That is the exact defect round 1 fixed in PremiumStopEditor, recreated in the sibling editor of the same number by the commit that fixed it. Both are fixed here (integer-cent arithmetic; the no-op guard hoisted above the range check), along with round 2's F10 (EditField's early return did not retire its message, so the two editors in one drawer had different rules for the same caution) and its false records. Round 2's F12 second half did NOT reproduce -- `next` quantises to 0.0001 of a fraction, which is exactly the 0.01 of a percent the renderer shows, so the two derivations cannot disagree. The code change stands as a defensive single-derivation and the comment says so rather than claiming a fix. NO ROUND 3. The cap is spent and both rounds cleared the gate; HEAD is now one commit beyond the last audited one and `audited_through` records that.

decisions.q: The three-user-visible-follow-up batch is 3 commits ahead of main, both capped rounds returned 0 GATE, suite green. Merge, or spend a third round? Round 2's own fix commit is unaudited and round 2 did find that round 1's fix had introduced two user-visible regressions.
decisions.a: MERGE. Kenneth chose it over a third round. The reasoning that decided it: the two-round cap exists precisely to stop at a defined point, and breaking it the first time it binds would mean it was never a cap. The same 'but the newest commit is unaudited' argument is true after every round -- that is the treadmill that cost rounds 7-11. Merged to main at 3ecf2a91.

decisions.q: Where should a contract's implied volatility come from for Phase A? Only Tradier returns per-contract implied_volatility; IBKR and Tastytrade return symbol-level IV RANK, a different quantity. A bracketed Black-Scholes solver already exists at market.py:928 (_compute_iv_bs) and is already wired into scan.py:603.
decisions.a: TRADIER FIRST, SOLVER AS FALLBACK. Use Tradier's per-contract IV where present; fall back to the existing _compute_iv_bs rather than building anything new (two earlier sessions proposed building a bracketed solver that already exists -- do not repeat that). SPLIT `iv` (per-strike implied volatility) from `ivRank` (a true percentile, NULL when genuinely unavailable) in the same change, which is what fixes the live scoring defect: market.py:1277 writes raw IV x100 into a field named for a percentile, 1291/1308 conditionally overwrite it with a real rank, and scan.py:610-616 broadcasts an ATM value across every strike -- all then compared against iv_rank_pass_max: 34 and hard_reject.max_iv_rank: 70.

decisions.q: When no genuine IV-rank source answers (Tradier-only, i.e. most symbols), what should the IV rule score against? Today market.py:1277 writes raw IV x100 into a field named ivRank, IBKR/Tastytrade conditionally overwrite it with a real percentile, and scan.py:598 feeds the ATM contract's value -- whichever quantity it happens to be -- into iv_rank_pass_max: 34 / iv_rank_caution_max: 55 / hard_reject max_iv_rank: 70.
decisions.a: TWO NAMED FIELDS, TWO THRESHOLD SETS. Carry `iv` (absolute implied volatility, per strike, 0-100 scale) and `ivRank` (a true percentile, NULL unless IBKR or Tastytrade answered) as separate fields. Score against whichever is present, PREFERRING the rank. The existing 34/55/70 numbers move to the ABSOLUTE-IV threshold set, because raw IV is what they have actually been judging all along -- so today's behaviour is preserved rather than silently changed, and the >70 hard reject keeps firing. A separate PERCENTILE threshold set is added for the rank path, defaulted to the same 34/55/70 and RECORDED AS UNMEASURED alongside Q7. Rejected alternatives and why: renormalising the weights on null, and scoring a neutral 50 on null, both silently retire the >70 hard reject for most symbols, so a genuinely expensive option would get no penalty and no rejection at all; renaming to `iv` with one threshold set leaves the rank path conflated, just less visibly.

decisions.q: Round 1 finding (d): spread_builder.choose_primary picked bear_call (credit, SHORT premium) vs bear_put (debit, LONG premium) from a basis-blind figure against one unqualified threshold (settingsStore ivRankThreshold: 50), with iv_basis computed two lines away at scan.py and not passed. CORRECTION to how round 1 framed the severity: BOTH structures are built and returned by _build_spreads -- the pick decides which is labelled primary_sp and which alt_sp, not which reaches a broker. The real consequences are (i) which structure the user is steered toward, and (ii) each structure has its own survival filter (bear_put needs debit <= 40% of width, bear_call needs credit >= min_credit), so if the one picked as primary fails its filter you get no primary where the other ordering would have given one.
decisions.a: BASIS-AWARE, WITH A SEPARATE ABSOLUTE THRESHOLD. choose_primary now takes iv + iv_basis + both thresholds. On a genuine rank, ivRankThreshold keeps its original meaning as a PERCENTILE ('vol is rich FOR THIS NAME, so sell it'). On an absolute IV -- most chains -- a separate ivAbsThreshold applies, defaulted to the same 50 so nothing changed on the day it shipped, and UNMEASURED like the percentile seeds and Q7. With no reading at all it returns bear_put as a DELIBERATE branch (defined risk, no short-premium assignment exposure when the vol regime is unknown) rather than as an artifact of `iv_rank or 0.0`, which mapped 'unknown' onto the lowest possible vol and also could not distinguish a legitimate 0 from None. settingsStore v23->v24 seeds ivAbsThreshold from the user's OWN ivRankThreshold, not the constant: someone who moved the old single knob meant that for the chains they actually see, which are the absolute ones. Rejected: keeping one threshold for both bases (leaves the conflation in the one place that picks a trade structure); ranking no primary unless a true rank exists (a product change needing a no-primary UI path); deferring (d) to main (would break the in-branch rule for a BLOCKING finding).

decisions.decision: Kenneth: rewrite audit_rule. It was not too theoretical, it was UNBOUNDED -- an exit criterion nobody can reach ('an adversarial reviewer has nothing left to say'), applied to batches too large to reach it with. Evidence that the project was not globally stalled: main took 150 commits in 12 days (26 Aug - 6 Sep, ~12/day, regular merges through 2 Sep). Evidence that the loop was: Phase A, 25 hours and 6 rounds unmerged; open_questions at 28 entries; Phase A's note field at 21,932 characters. Four changes: severity floor for the reviewer, target shrinks to what changed since the last round, objective exit (one zero-finding round), and smaller batches. A three-round hard cap escalates to Kenneth rather than running a fourth. REFINEMENT ON WHAT WAS PROPOSED: the proposal said 'two consecutive zero-BLOCKING rounds'. Written out, the second round is redundant -- a zero-finding round triggers no fixes, so it injects nothing for a further round to catch, and the round that reviewed the previous fixes already WAS the second look. Kenneth to confirm; revert to two-consecutive if he prefers the stricter form.

decisions.q: What order should the remaining work run in, given Phase B is half-built, one commit on the branch is unaudited, and three approved UI items are unstarted?
decisions.a: LOCKED, in this order and no other. (1) ADVERSARIAL AUDIT of 5aac0027 ('Render the stop-vs-premium gate instead of computing it') FIRST -- it is unaudited code that changes how the max-loss figure reaches the screen, which is squarely inside audit_rule's gate, and it must not be merged over. Use K-adversarial-audit-loop, audit-only, scoped to THAT COMMIT alone per audit_rule v2's shrinking-target clause -- NOT the cumulative branch diff. (2) THEN FINISH PHASE B, batches 2 and 3 of 3. Batch 1 is built and clean; a half-applied pricing basis means part of the card grades on Black-Scholes and part on the old delta-linear ruler, which is the exact silent-mismatch class that has already produced two wrong-number defects. Keep batches separate and audit each -- audit_rule v2's batch-size clause (~500 lines / one layer) is why batch 1 cleared in two rounds. (3) THEN MERGE to main. NOT NOW, and specifically not before (1). DEFERRED, explicitly and not forgotten: the three approved UI builds (EDITED-FLAG, TARGET-VINTAGE, ALERT-THRESHOLD-STAMP) -- all approved, all small, none of them produces a wrong number, so they rank below a half-built pricing basis. Phase C is unblocked (A is clean and merged) but stays unstarted: two open fronts is the limit.

decisions.a: KEEP claude/retrieve-instance-environment-2cysxj. DELETE claude/dev-state-reconstruction-hzmzbi. This was never a real fork: verified 2026-09-08 with `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/claude/dev-state-reconstruction-hzmzbi HEAD`, which passed -- the old branch (1bf9a599, 3 commits ahead of main) is FULLY CONTAINED in the current branch (5aac0027, 4 ahead). decisions.a: NO -- THE PREMISE INVERTED, AND THE DELETE IS NO LONGER SAFE. The decision was correct when made: hzmzbi's tip was 1bf9a599 and 2cysxj contained it. What neither session could see is that hzmzbi had an UNPUSHED commit -- the approved open-questions triage -- so the containment check ran against a stale remote. Both sessions were also live at once, on two accounts, in two containers: 2cysxj built and audited B2 while hzmzbi applied the triage. Resolved 2026-09-08 by rebasing the triage onto 2cysxj's tip (0a4d8dc6) and keeping the result on hzmzbi, so hzmzbi = every B2 commit + the triage, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/claude/retrieve-instance-environment-2cysxj HEAD` now passes in the OTHER direction. Nothing was lost and no commit was rewritten except the triage's own replay. STANDING RULE THIS COST US: verify containment against a FETCHED remote AND the local tip of both names, never one of them -- a `--is-ancestor` check is only ever a claim about the refs you actually have. Kenneth still owns which NAME survives; until he says, delete neither.  ---- SUPERSEDED 2026-09-08 by BRANCH-NAME-FINAL-2026-09-08, which settles the name.

decisions.q: B3's ranking badge (gate-basis spec 2.3) has to be priced against a scan-time stop, and no such stop exists: scan.py never calls compute_final_stop (verified -- its only caller anywhere is routers/contracts.py:942, the exit-plan endpoint), and the only stop the scan produces is exit.invalidation, which trade_plan.py:119-121 derives as a FLAT percentage stock move from risk_rules.yaml's bullish/bearish_invalidation_pct ('-3% stock = invalidation'), not a structural or ATR level. Pricing the badge against that would grade every candidate at a stop the app is on record as wanting to replace. The two source documents also disagree on who owns the badge: the gate-basis spec (2026-09-02) 2.3 puts it in Phase B, and the later consolidated implementation plan (2026-09-03) puts it in Phase C part 5. Plan 7 resolves the BASIS conflict between those documents (Black-Scholes wins) but never the OWNERSHIP one. How is it resolved?
decisions.a: SCOPED SCAN-TIME STOP, AND PHASE B FINISHES NOW. Compute the stop inside the scan for the auto-picked contract only -- `compute_final_stop(candles, direction, price, atr, atr_multiplier)`, the same wider-of-structural-or-ATR-floor function the exit-plan endpoint already uses -- and price the gate on it with `compute_stop_cost`. SCOPED means exactly that and no more: Phase C's piece 3 stays unbuilt, `exit.invalidation` is NOT repointed, and nothing else on the card changes basis. The badge gets a real stop; the flat -3% keeps its existing consumers until Phase C replaces it deliberately. The ownership conflict resolves toward the EARLIER document (Phase B) because the badge is the last surface still ungated after B2, and leaving it to Phase C would ship a release where the card grades on Black-Scholes and the ranking table grades on nothing. Everything it needs was verified present: ContractDetails.iv is on the wire (Phase A), compute_stop_cost is importable, candles and the auto-picked contract are both in scope at the assembly point in _process_symbol, and cardToRow builds WatchlistRow at render time so only scanStore needs a version bump.
decisions.provenance: RECONSTRUCTED, and flagged as such deliberately. Kenneth answered this in a session that hit its usage limit mid-build and whose container was never pushed; the record here was rebuilt from screenshots of that conversation, in which the question and the chosen option label ('Scoped stop, finish B now') are both legible. The chosen label maps to exactly one implementation given what the code makes available, so the reconstruction carries no discretion -- but Kenneth has not re-confirmed the wording, and the B3 work built on it should be treated as resting on a reconstructed decision until he does. The analysis it rests on was NOT taken from the screenshots on trust: compute_final_stop's caller set, trade_plan.py:119-121's flat percentage, cardToRow's render-time construction and WatchlistRow's missing fields were each re-verified in the code first.

decisions.q: BRANCH-RESOLUTION-AMENDED-2026-09-08 left the surviving branch NAME open, because containment had inverted and both names held work. Which name survives?
decisions.a: KEEP claude/dev-state-reconstruction-hzmzbi. DELETE claude/retrieve-instance-environment-2cysxj. Two reasons, and the first is the one that matters: hzmzbi is the only branch carrying every commit, and it is the name this session's own instructions designate as the push target. 2cysxj is one commit behind and holds nothing unique. Containment re-verified against a FRESHLY FETCHED remote immediately before the delete -- `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/claude/retrieve-instance-environment-2cysxj HEAD` passed -- which is the check BRANCH-RESOLUTION-2026-09-08 got wrong by running it against a stale remote. THE DELETE HAS NOT HAPPENED YET AND IS KENNETH'S TO DO: `git push origin --delete claude/retrieve-instance-environment-2cysxj` was REFUSED from this environment with HTTP 403 (the session's git credentials allow pushes but not branch deletions; the agent proxy was healthy, so this is a GitHub-side permission, not a transport failure). Delete it from the GitHub branches page instead. It is safe whenever it happens: its four B2 commits (5aac0027, 65a5443f, 4ffdef62, 0a4d8dc6) are all reachable from hzmzbi. Until then TWO NAMES EXIST ON THE REMOTE and 2cysxj is the stale one -- do not branch from it or push to it. THIS SUPERSEDES BRANCH-RESOLUTION-2026-09-08 entirely -- that decision's answer is now the opposite of the standing one, and it is kept only for the record of how the mistake happened.

decisions.q: Phase B's code is complete but B3 has had zero adversarial rounds. Audit now, or merge and audit later?
decisions.a: AUDIT B3 FIRST. NOTHING MERGES TO MAIN UNTIL A ROUND COMES BACK CLEAN. This is the project's standing rule applied without exception, and B3 is the worst possible place to make one: it puts a percentage and a verdict on EVERY row of the ranking table, which is the screen candidates are chosen from, so a wrong number there is silently acted on before any card is ever opened. It is also the only unaudited code on the branch -- batch 1 and B2 are each clean after 2 rounds -- so the audit target is small and the round should be cheap. Use K-adversarial-audit-loop, audit-only, scoped to commit 8891ecfe ALONE per audit_rule v2's shrinking-target clause, NOT the cumulative branch diff. Fix every GATE-level finding in-branch and log the rest against main. When it comes back clean: set Phase B status to 'shipped' and audit_clean to true, THEN merge -- which completes WORK-ORDER-2026-09-08 step 3.

decisions.q: Merge claude/deferred-ui-builds-2026-09-08 (6 commits, based on current main, no rebase needed) to main as it stands?
decisions.a: NO, NOT AS IT STANDS -- and then YES once one round is run. Five of the six commits are audit-clean (EDITED-FLAG 2 rounds, TARGET-VINTAGE 1 round). The sixth, 5fc4d5e9 (ALERT-THRESHOLD-STAMP), has ZERO. Merging now would break audit_rule on precisely the item that skipped it. Do NOT split the branch to merge the clean five: that costs two merges and a broken audit trail for no gain, and the work is already safe on the remote so there is no time pressure. Audit 5fc4d5e9 ALONE, fix any gate-level finding in-branch, then merge all six with --no-ff. Verified green at decision time: typecheck clean, frontend 110 suites / 1349 tests. Backend untouched by this branch.

decisions.q: A trade card whose stop is null (a candidate restored from a pre-piece-3 scan, stripped by the scanStore v15 migration) can still be ordered via the two DIRECT buttons -- 'Place Limit' and 'Right Now - Market' -- because `checkTradeRisk`'s `missing_invalidation` runs only inside SendToBrokerDialog, the basket path. The position is stored with `PortfolioPosition.stop = null` and therefore ARMS NO STOP ALERT until the user sets one in the portfolio EditDrawer. Nothing fires at a wrong level (both alert engines skip a null stop) -- the position simply goes unwatched, looking normal in the portfolio list. Gate the two direct buttons on the same check, or let the order through and mark the position?
decisions.a: APPROVED -- GATE THE TWO DIRECT BUTTONS. Kenneth chose the refusal over the marker: the exposure window is narrow (only cards from a scan run before piece 3; a fresh scan cannot produce a null stop, since the backend always sends a number -- the resolved stop or the flat fallback), the workaround is 'run a scan', and a position quietly going unwatched is discovered at the worst possible moment. NOT YET BUILT. Scope when it is: refuse 'Place Limit' and 'Right Now - Market' on a card whose RESOLVED stop is null -- resolved, not `card.exit.invalidation`, so a stop the user has typed still unblocks it exactly as it does on the basket path (that is why `checkTradeRisk` gained `resolvedInvalidation` in C2). Same refusal copy as the dialog's, and the AutoTradeArm path needs the same check or it becomes the new hole -- its own comment at components/organisms/AutoTradeArm/index.tsx:237 already notes it arms no alerts where Place Limit threads both. Build it on a NEW branch off a main that ALREADY CARRIES PHASE C: it touches app/(frame)/screener/step-7-trade-card/page.tsx, which C2 changed.

decisions.q: recommendedShares sizes off the risk budget exactly as the piece-6 spec mandates (floor(risk_budget / riskPerShare), spec test 6) but never consults portfolio.max_single_position_pct (0.05). On the AAPL fixture -- entry 211.59, stop 195.90, $3,750 budget at the default 3.75% of $100k -- it returns 239 shares, a ~$50,570 position against a 5% cap of $5,000, i.e. ~10x over and about 23 shares by the cap. The two rules answer different questions (how much do I lose if wrong, vs how much of the account sits in one name) and a TIGHTER stop makes the gap WIDER. Barely visible on options because an option's premium is both the notional and close to the whole risk. Cap the number, flag it, or leave it as pure risk-budget sizing?
decisions.a: APPROVED -- OPTION 2, FLAG IT. Keep recommending the risk-budget number and warn when it exceeds max_single_position_pct; do NOT clamp. Rejected capping because it silently overrules a number the spec mandates and would make the recommendation useless on any liquid large-cap with a tight stop; rejected leaving it because the implied-notional line already shipped beside the share count and is easy to skim past next to a bold share number. Same shape as DIRECT-SEND-STOP-GATE: make the conflict impossible to miss, leave the choice with the trader. NOT YET BUILT. Scope when it is: the warning belongs on the StockPositionCard beside the existing 'SHARES 239 / ~$50570 position' readout (frontend/components/organisms/StockPositionCard/index.tsx:890-896); it must compare against the SAME portfolio value and cap the risk checks use (riskStore maxSingleTradeExposurePct / portfolioValue, NOT a second copy of 0.05), and it must not block the Apply button -- flag, not gate. Backend recommendedShares (routers/stock_scan.py:1894-1897) stays exactly as the spec pins it.

decisions.q: Spec section 6.1: does v0 seed from the chain's MEAN IV or the ATM strike? And Kenneth's sharper question behind it -- why guess at all when the chain already carries the variance, and can we keep the whole per-strike variance instead of collapsing it to one number?
decisions.a: SEED FROM THE CHAIN'S MEAN IV. Log the ATM alternative as UNMEASURED, in the same register as Phase A's seeded-but-unmeasured IV thresholds. Mean won both reference chains (45 DTE 0.0796 vs ATM 0.0919; 180 DTE 0.3163 vs 0.3744), which is the OPPOSITE of what theory predicts -- the 180-DTE delta band reaches far enough into the wings to pull the mean up toward the smile -- and one synthetic chain does not settle a question that contradicts theory. Ship the measured winner, record that it is one measurement. || THE PREMISE OF THE QUESTION IS RIGHT AND WORTH WRITING DOWN, because it is the thing most likely to be misread later: F2 IS NOT GUESSING v0. Today's shipped code guesses -- v0_grid=[0.04] is a hardcoded 20% vol applied to every symbol, and the 45-DTE reference chain's own IV says 0.1245 (35.28% vol), so no setting of the shipped code can seed it correctly. F2 replaces the guess with a value SOLVED OUT OF THE CHAIN'S OWN MIDS. 'Mean vs ATM' is only which single reading the search starts from. || WHY IT CANNOT BE THE WHOLE PER-STRIKE VARIANCE: v0 is the INSTANTANEOUS variance and is one scalar by definition. The chain gives many IVs, one per strike -- that spread IS the smile, and in Heston the smile is what the OTHER FOUR parameters (kappa, theta, sigma_v, rho) exist to produce out of that single v0. So the chain's full smile is NOT discarded: every strike of it is the calibration target. Giving each strike its own variance would not be a better Heston fit, it would be no model at all -- that is Black-Scholes at each contract's own IV, which reproduces every mid BY CONSTRUCTION (measured RMSE 0.000005, section 0a/3.3's 'degenerate' note) and predicts nothing for a strike or a date nobody quoted. Repricing a contract at a stop, which is what this whole engine is for, is exactly an off-chain question.

decisions.q: Spec sections 6.2 and 4: widen or refine the grid now, given that three of five parameters pin at a boundary and the winner violates Feller (2*kappa*theta=0.08 < sigma_v^2=0.36)? And is there any action to take on the edge-of-the-box finding beyond recording it?
decisions.a: DO NOT WIDEN THE GRID IN F2. Kenneth took the spec's recommendation. Widening is a LATENCY decision, it is a second change, and section 3.3's flat-BS baseline gate already makes a bad fit harmless -- a fit worse than one flat volatility returns method='bs_flat' and never reaches a card. Revisit as its own measured change after F2 lands; the measurement already in hand is that anchoring theta to [0.5x, 1x, 2x] the seed takes the 45-DTE fit from rel-RMSE 0.0919 to 0.0700 for 50% more combos (16 -> 24, 0.24s -> 0.36s), and theta STILL lands on the top rung. || THE EDGE OF THE BOX AND FELLER ARE NOTED, NOT ACTED ON -- with ONE cheap addition to F2's own scope, which is the only new thing decided here: LOG WHEN A WINNING PARAMETER LANDS ON A GRID BOUNDARY. Same reasoning as the ladder-floor logging decided alongside it. It costs nothing, and it converts 'three of five pinned' from a one-off observation on ONE SYNTHETIC CHAIN into accumulating evidence from Kenneth's real scans -- which is precisely what the widening decision needs and does not have. Without it, revisiting section 6.2 later means re-running the same synthetic measurement and learning nothing new.  ---- THE LOGGING HALF IS SUPERSEDED 2026-09-13 by BOUNDARY-LOG-GATE-ON-GRID-2026-09-13: the log this decision added cannot produce the evidence it was added for, because the shipped grid makes every winner a boundary winner by construction. The decision NOT to widen the grid in F2 stands.

decisions.q: F1 proved the ladder floor in reward_risk.py (214-260) guards against a dip that was the Fourier-inversion defect itself, so it now has no known mechanism to catch and is a MASK rather than a guard -- a dip reaching it most likely means the pricer regressed, and the floor would quietly raise the level instead of surfacing it. Remove it, keep it, or keep it and make it visible?
decisions.a: KEEP THE FLOOR AND MAKE IT LOG WHEN IT FIRES. Not removed: spec section 4 and 6.3 both say 'no artifact on this fixture' is not 'no artifact on any live chain', and the floor only ever RAISES a level, so keeping it cannot produce a too-low target. But keeping it silent is what makes it a mask, so it stops being silent. The log line is the mechanism by which the live evidence accumulates on its own, instead of waiting for someone to go looking for it -- which is what section 6.3's 'remove it only after F1 has run against live chains long enough' otherwise depends on and has no way to deliver. || PROCESS NOTE, recorded because the turn it came from is not in any transcript: this option was put to Kenneth as '(a)' in a session whose context was lost, and he answered 'agree take (a)'. The next session RESTATED the reading in plain words -- keep the floor, add logging -- before acting on it, and he confirmed by approving the log. If (a) meant something else, this decision is the thing to correct.

decisions.q: Spec section 4 lists three observations deliberately outside F2: _CALIBRATION_TIMEOUT does not bound latency, the lru_cache key is redundant and spot-sensitive, and heston_iv is dead code. Do any of them get done, and is any of them a major issue for Bamendjou?
decisions.a: LEAVE ALL THREE. NONE IS MAJOR -- none can put a wrong number in front of a user or on a broker order, which is audit_rule's own gate, so all three are exactitude rather than risk. (1) _CALIBRATION_TIMEOUT: calibrate_cached's ThreadPoolExecutor block calls shutdown(wait=True), so the except TimeoutError branch still blocks for the full grid search -- a LATENCY bug, already worked around at the only call site (scan.py's asyncio.wait, which does not cancel), and F1 made the grid CHEAPER (0.56s -> 0.35s on the realistic chain), so the pressure went down, not up. (2) the lru_cache key: chain_repr already determines iv_key and S is unrounded, so a one-cent spot move is a cache miss -- pure wasted CPU, and finding #6 of the slowness investigation already found the cache rarely helps anyway. (3) heston_iv: computes h_price, tests it, returns bs_iv on both branches, no caller outside heston.py -- a delete. || IF THEY ARE EVER DONE, BUNDLE THEM THAT WAY: (1) and (2) are both in heston_cache.py and are both about latency, so they are one small change, worth making only if scan speed actually starts bothering Kenneth. (3) is two lines in heston.py and should ride along with the forward-intrinsic clamp tightening already logged in open_questions, which is the other 'next time anyone is in heston.py' item. || THE ONE TO WATCH IS NOT ON THAT LIST. heston_price wraps its quad calls in bare `except Exception`, and Warning subclasses Exception, so in any process that escalates warnings to errors scipy's IntegrationWarning makes it silently return bs_price while every downstream label still reads 'Heston repriced' -- demonstrated bit-identical at v0=0.01/kappa=0.5/theta=0.02/sigma_v=0.6/rho=-0.8, 30 DTE. Unreachable TODAY because nothing in this app escalates warnings. It becomes reachable the day anyone adds -W error to CI or a library calls simplefilter('error'). That one is a mislabelled number, not exactitude. Its open_questions entry stands; this decision raises its priority above the three above. || AND THE GENUINELY MAJOR ITEM IS F2 ITSELF: post-F1 the card still prices 27%-100% BELOW the market mid across the ranked band and labels it 'Heston repriced'.  ---- PARTLY SUPERSEDED 2026-09-13 by TIMEOUT-DELETE-INNER-2026-09-13. This decision filed `_CALIBRATION_TIMEOUT does not bound latency` as exactitude, reasoning that F1 made the grid cheaper so the pressure went DOWN. True for F1, FALSE for F2, which adds the baseline sweep to the same budget -- measured 0.834s pre-F2 to ~1.05s post-F2 on the 180-DTE reference chain, against a 1.0s budget. The other two items (the lru_cache key, dead heston_iv) stand as filed.

decisions.q: F2's audit showed `_CALIBRATION_TIMEOUT = 1.0` discarding fits that BEAT the flat-BS baseline -- the 180-DTE reference chain at ~1.05s, and under concurrency even a 0.325s 45-DTE chain on 8 of 8 calls. Raise it, make it cancel properly, delete it, or leave it?
decisions.a: DELETE THE INNER TIMEOUT. Not tune it -- remove it. THE REASON IS THAT THERE ARE TWO TIMEOUTS STACKED AND ONLY THE OUTER ONE WORKS, verified by reading both files: scan.py:287 sets `_HESTON_CALIBRATION_TIMEOUT_S = 2.0` and waits on the task with `asyncio.wait`, which does NOT cancel -- it moves on and lets the calibration finish in the background. That is what actually bounds scan latency, and it does it correctly. heston_cache.py:397-403 then adds its own 1.0s `future.result(timeout=...)` INSIDE a `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...)` block whose __exit__ calls shutdown(wait=True) -- so the call blocks for the full grid search ANYWAY and then throws the finished result away. It saves no time and costs the answer. It is also STRICTER than the guard that does the work (1.0s vs 2.0s), which is why the 180-DTE chain at ~1.05s is discarded by the inner one and would have been accepted comfortably by the outer. || MEASURE BEFORE DELETING, and this is a condition of the decision rather than a nicety: take the real latency spread across a full scan first. If chains routinely run past 2s then the OUTER budget is the thing to revisit and this decision is wrong; the evidence so far is two synthetic chains (0.30s at 45 DTE, ~1.05s at 180 DTE, 2.25s inner / 2.38s wall at 55 strikes) and that is not a distribution. || Its own change, off the merged main, with its own adversarial round. Expected effect: Heston reappears on long-dated cards, where F2's improvement is currently computed and then discarded.  ---- MEASURED 2026-09-13, BEFORE DELETING, as this decision required. THE CONDITION IT SET FOR BEING WRONG WAS PARTLY MET, and Kenneth chose to proceed anyway with the rest logged. Harness: backend/scripts/heston_latency_probe.py (committed with the change, so every number below is re-runnable -- and SHOULD be re-run on Kenneth's machine, which has more cores than the 4-core 2.1GHz Xeon these came from). || (1) THE SPREAD, solo: 0.163s (21 DTE, 8 strikes) to 1.733s (270 DTE, 60 strikes) across 45 shapes, median 0.607s. NOT ONE solo shape exceeds 2.0s, so on that reading the outer budget looked fine. || (2) IT IS NOT FINE, and this is the finding that reframes the decision: a staggered 40-symbol scan slice driven through scan.py's own machinery abandons 40 OF 40 SYMBOLS at the 2.0s outer guard -- median wait 2.01s, not one symbol completing in time, no Heston number reaching any card at all. Chains DO routinely run past 2s under scan concurrency, which is the clause this decision named as making it wrong. || (3) WHY, and it is not chain cost: calibration is GIL-BOUND, so `_HESTON_EXECUTOR` buys NEGATIVE parallelism -- 2 threads measured 2.48-2.58x one thread's wall time, 4 threads 5.43-5.54x, 8 threads 10.57-11.34x, ON 4 IDLE CORES. `heston_price` integrates a PYTHON integrand through scipy's QUADPACK, so the GIL is held nearly throughout. The 2.0s is spent queueing, not calibrating, and widening it does not fix that. || (4) THE DELETION STILL EARNS ITS PLACE, on the narrower claim the measurement actually supports: with the outer guard removed so the inner timeout was the only thing in play, the same 40 symbols went from 40/40 `bs_fallback` to 40/40 `heston_grid`. CORRECTED 2026-09-13 by adversarial round 2, which caught the probe holding the scan semaphore ACROSS the calibration when the real `_process_symbol` releases it before the Heston block (scan.py:600 vs 728-816) -- so the first model capped in-flight calibrations at 5 and UNDERSTATED contention. Remeasured with the semaphore released at the right point: median wait 17.7s before / 16.8s after, minimum 3.75s / 3.66s (the earlier, wrong figures were 3.46s and 1.65s). The before half was rerun against this block reconstructed verbatim, so it is a genuine before/after under ONE contention model rather than two readings. The 40/40 -> 40/40 verdict is unchanged and the guarded verdict is unchanged at 40/40 abandoned. Same work, same wall time, 40 fits kept instead of 40 computed and thrown away. ON THE MEASURING BOX IT MOVES NO CARD -- with the real guard in place it is 40/40 abandoned both before and after -- and the in-code comment says exactly that rather than the flattering version. An earlier draft of this change claimed '6 of 40 now reach a card'; that was read off the UNGUARDED run and the guarded run refused it. || SO THE DECISION'S STATED EXPECTED EFFECT -- 'Heston reappears on long-dated cards' -- IS NOT DELIVERED BY THIS CHANGE and nothing here should be read as claiming it. It is a precondition for delivering it. The blocker is now logged as its own open question (the GIL one).  ---- CLEAN AFTER 2 ADVERSARIAL ROUNDS, both ZERO gate-level findings, on claude/heston-timeout-inner-2026-09-13. Round 2 was run deliberately against audit_rule v2's one-clean-round exit, on the same reasoning the F2 session used: that clause justifies itself by 'the round that reviewed the last batch of fixes was already the second look', and a round 1 that finds nothing produces no fixes, so there was no second look to inherit. Round 1 re-derived the 'it bounded nothing' claim by executing the deleted block (2.00s elapsed on a 2.0s job, returning bs_fallback), confirmed a single production caller, and reproduced every committed number. Round 2 ran 17 mutations (11 killed, 6 survived -- 4 equivalent or unreachable, 2 on the pre-existing `len(chain) < 3` boundary this diff does not touch, logged separately), traced newly-admitted fits through estimate_rr/estimate_targets across 96 chain cells finding no negative premium, no inverted ladder and no R/R sign flip this diff introduces, and confirmed nothing Heston-derived reaches a broker order (entry, invalidation and premium_stop all come from elsewhere in trade_plan.py; only rr_ratio, rr_model and targets[].estimatedOptionPrice are Heston-influenced, all display-only). THREE BELOW-GATE ITEMS WERE ACTED ON RATHER THAN LOGGED, because each was a defect in THIS change's own artifacts rather than a 'while I am here': the understating probe above; a stale present-tense description of the deleted timeout at scan.py:241-246 that the commit corrected at :790-798 and missed; and a trailing newline json.dump had stripped from this file.

decisions.q: F2's audit showed `_boundary_hits` is tautological on the grid that ships -- two rungs per searched dimension means every winner is at a min or a max by construction, 16 of 16 enumerated, so the count is always 4 and only the side varies. That also makes its guard effectively unconditional: about 500 WARNING lines per S&P 500 scan, in the same stream as the ladder-floor warning added so a pricer regression would be NOTICED. Reshape it, log the side pattern, delete it, or leave it?
decisions.a: LOG ONLY WHEN THE GRID HAS MORE THAN TWO RUNGS IN THE DIMENSION CONCERNED. Roughly a one-line condition. It goes silent today -- correctly, because today's output carries no information -- and it wakes up by itself the day the grid is widened, which is exactly when decision F2-GRID-AND-EDGE-OF-BOX-2026-09-13 wants the evidence. Under HESTON_FULL_CALIBRATION=1 (3 rungs) the count is already informative: 80/81 combos hit at least one boundary, 16/81 hit all four. || NOT deleted, because the diagnostic is the right idea and only its trigger is wrong. NOT reshaped to log the side pattern: that is more code for evidence nobody has asked a question of yet, and the grid-widening decision is the only consumer. || Carry the fix to `test_winner_on_a_grid_boundary_is_logged` with it -- its four-parameter assertion is true for every possible outcome on the shipped grid, so only its `'v0' not in ...` clause discriminates today.

decisions.q: Six scoping questions for Phase G (piece 5, the per-trade method pick): scope, interaction with auto-trade arming, what persists, whether the pick reaches the backend, whether it gates sending, and whether it cascades.
decisions.a: (Q1) SCOPE IS BOTH MODES -- options AND stocks. (Q2) THE PICK IS FROZEN AT ARM TIME -- CORRECTED 2026-09-14, see q2_correction below; the first answer was 'read live at fire time' and it was taken on an option description that understated the cost. (Q3) THE SIBLING CACHES COME WITH THE SELECTION; it does not persist alone. (Q4) THE PICK REACHES THE BACKEND AT SEND TIME AND IS PERSISTED ON THE POSITION, so the portfolio can later show which method a trade was judged on. (Q5) AN EXPLICIT PICK IS REQUIRED BEFORE A TRADE CAN BE SENT -- send is blocked until a method is chosen; nothing goes out on a default nobody looked at. (Q6) NO CASCADE IN G.
decisions.provenance: PARTLY RECONSTRUCTED, and flagged because the reconstruction was FORCED. The six questions were put to Kenneth in a session whose context was lost and WERE NEVER WRITTEN DOWN -- no G spec exists on any branch, and the state file carried no record of them. His answers survived as bare letters ('(b)', '(a)', 'agree with proposition'), which are meaningless without the option lists. Q1, Q3 and Q6 were recovered from the wording of his own reply (he answered those in words, and Q3's question text enumerates its two options in order). Q2, Q4 and Q5 could NOT be recovered and were RE-ASKED, with option sets rebuilt from the code rather than invented -- Q2 from AutoTradeArm's existing freeze-at-arm design, Q4 from what persisting would actually cost, Q5 from the precedent of the regime REJECT gate. This is the SECOND time a lost session's scoping decisions had to be reconstructed (the first was B3-SCOPED-STOP-2026-09-08). The lesson both times: write the QUESTION down with the answer, because a letter without its option list is not a record.
decisions.q2_correction: Q2 WAS ANSWERED TWICE AND THE FIRST ANSWER WAS MINE TO FIX, not Kenneth's. He first chose 'read live at fire time' from an option I wrote, which said only that it DIVERGED from auto-trade's existing freeze-at-arm design. That understated it, and he re-opened the question by asking what the CONSISTENT choice was. Checking the code rather than the design intent produced three facts the option should have carried: (1) THERE IS NO CLIENT AT FIRE TIME. `fire_now()` in routers/auto_trade.py:51 TAKES NO REQUEST BODY -- it fires whatever ArmedStrategy was captured by /auto-trade/arm. The browser is not in the loop and the card need not even be open, so there is no live pick to read. 'Live at fire' would require inventing a channel that pushes the pick to the backend on every change and having fire read it: a SECOND mechanism on top of G's, and outside G's scope. (2) THE METHOD CANNOT CHANGE THE ORDER. ArmRequest (auto_trade.py:15-33) carries broker, symbol, option_symbol, action, quantity, order_type, limit_price, conid, entry_premium, portfolio_value and premium_stop_pct -- NO method field, and nothing in the submitted order depends on one. The pricing method moves DISPLAYED numbers (R/R, target prices), not what is bought. So the two answers cannot differ in what reaches the broker at all. (3) WHAT IS ACTUALLY AT STAKE IS THE RECORD, and only because Q4 persists the method on the position: WHICH method is written against the trade. Frozen-at-arm records the method that was on screen when Kenneth committed to the trade. Live-at-fire would record whatever happened to be showing at a moment he was not present for. SO THE CORRECTED ANSWER REMOVES THE INCONSISTENCY RATHER THAN DOCUMENTING IT: quantity, premium stop and now the method are all captured at arm, one rule for the whole card, and the spec has nothing to explain away. AutoTradeArm/index.tsx:22's existing note -- that a later edit does not change what 'Fire now' submits -- now covers the method too.

decisions.q: EDITED-FLAG's card-level 'edited' indicator watches `targets` as a SEVENTH field, which the original decision's parenthetical (Entry limit, Max fill, Contracts, Premium stop, Time stop, Invalidation) does not name. It was included because TargetRow calls patch({targets}) today, so omitting it would print 'not edited' on a card whose targets had just been retyped. Keep the seventh field or remove it?
decisions.a: KEEP IT. Confirmed by Kenneth 2026-09-14, closing an item that had been open since the 2026-09-09 merge. The indicator answers 'has anything on this card been changed from what the scan produced', and a retyped target IS such a change -- printing 'not edited' over one would be the indicator lying about the card it sits on. The original parenthetical was an enumeration of the fields known at the time, not a closed set. No code change: it has shipped this way since 0b057b0a and now has the decision to match.

*** CORRECTED 2026-09-18: THE FIX PRESCRIBED BELOW NAMES A BRANCH NO REAL TRADE EVER TAKES, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE PIECE. *** The entry below diagnoses the defect as `100 - conviction` on the SELL branch and prescribes `-conviction`.
